question: How much weight did participants lose on tirzepatide in the SURMOUNT-1 trial, and over how long?
answer: In SURMOUNT-1, adults with obesity or overweight (without diabetes) took once-weekly tirzepatide or placebo for 72 weeks alongside a lifestyle intervention [1][2]. At week 72 the mean change in body weight was -15.0% with the 5 mg dose, -19.5% with 10 mg, and -20.9% with 15 mg, compared with -3.1% on placebo [1]. About 50% of participants on 10 mg and 57% on 15 mg lost 20% or more of their body weight, versus 3% on placebo [1]. These are the treatment-regimen estimates from the published paper. An on-treatment (efficacy) analysis gives somewhat different, larger numbers, so it matters which analysis is being quoted [1]. A longer follow-up in participants with prediabetes reached 176 weeks and reported mean weight changes of -12.3% (5 mg), -18.7% (10 mg) and -19.7% (15 mg) versus -1.3% with placebo. That population differs from the original trial, so it is not a direct comparison [3].

question: What are the main side effects reported for semaglutide in clinical trials?
answer: The main side effects of semaglutide 2.4 mg in the STEP weight-management trials are gastrointestinal. In pooled STEP 1-3 data, nausea affected 43.9% of semaglutide users versus 16.1% on placebo, diarrhoea 29.7% versus 15.9%, vomiting 24.5% versus 6.3%, and constipation 24.2% versus 11.1% [1]. Most of these events were non-serious (99.5%) and mild to moderate (98.1%). They were usually transient and occurred most often during or shortly after dose escalation [1]. About 4.3% of semaglutide-treated participants permanently stopped the drug because of GI events [1]. The STEP 1 registry record shows the same pattern, with nausea in 44.1% versus 17.4% on placebo and vomiting in 24.6% versus 6.6% [2]. In STEP 6, which used lower doses, rates were lower. Nausea was about 17.6-18.0% versus 4.0% on placebo, and vomiting 8.5-10.0% versus 2.0% [3]. Rates vary with the trial, population and dose.

question: What does the current evidence say about intermittent fasting compared with daily calorie restriction for weight loss?
answer: The evidence mostly points to intermittent fasting and daily (continuous) calorie restriction producing similar weight loss. The largest recent analysis is a 2025 BMJ network meta-analysis of 99 randomised trials with 6,582 adults [1][2]. It found that all intermittent fasting strategies and continuous energy restriction reduced body weight compared with an unrestricted (ad libitum) diet [1][2]. Alternate-day fasting was the only strategy that beat continuous restriction, by about 1.29 kg (95% CI -1.99 to -0.59), with moderate certainty of evidence. That gap did not reach the authors' threshold of 2 kg for a clinically important difference [2]. Other fasting types, such as time-restricted eating and whole-day fasting, showed trivial differences from each other [2]. An accompanying editorial noted that many comparisons were against ad libitum diets, and the authors said longer trials are needed [2]. An earlier 2022 review in Nutrients suggested intermittent fasting may be superior to continuous calorie restriction in some respects, but its authors described the question as still controversial [3]. Overall the results are mixed but lean toward equivalence, and most participants in the trials had existing health conditions.

question: How effective is the RSV vaccine for adults over 60 according to the trial data?
answer: Two pivotal phase 3 trials in adults aged 60 and older found substantial efficacy, but the figures depend on the endpoint and follow-up period. In the GSK trial of the adjuvanted RSVPreF3 OA vaccine (Arexvy), efficacy against RT-PCR-confirmed RSV lower respiratory tract disease was 82.6% over a median follow-up of 6.7 months, with 7 cases in the vaccine group versus 40 on placebo [1][2]. Efficacy was 71.7% against RSV-related acute respiratory infection and 94.1% against severe RSV lower respiratory tract disease [2]. Estimates for adults 80 and older and for frail adults were less certain [1]. In a later analysis of the same trial, a single dose kept about 48% efficacy in the third season, so protection waned over time [3]. In Pfizer's trial of the bivalent RSVpreF vaccine (Abrysvo), efficacy was 66.7% against RSV lower respiratory tract illness with at least 2 symptoms [4]. It was 85.7% against illness with at least 3 symptoms [5]. A second-season analysis reported about 81.5% (95% CI 63.3-91.6) efficacy for the 3-symptom endpoint [6]. The two trials used different endpoints and populations, so their numbers should not be compared directly.

question: What is the recommended daily sodium intake for adults according to the WHO, and how much do people actually consume?
answer: The WHO recommends that adults consume less than 2,000 mg of sodium per day, equivalent to less than 5 g of salt, or just under a teaspoon [1][3]. People consume far more. The WHO's Sodium reduction fact sheet puts the global mean adult intake at 4,278 mg of sodium per day in 2021, equivalent to about 11 g of salt, which is more than double the recommended limit [1]. An earlier WHO news release from 2023 gave the global average as 10.8 g of salt per day [2]. If you cite the fact sheet itself, use the roughly 11 g figure.

question: What did the large trials find about low-dose aspirin for primary prevention of heart attacks in older adults?
answer:
The largest trial in older adults, ASPREE (published in the New England Journal of Medicine in September 2018), found that low-dose aspirin did not meaningfully lower heart attack risk in healthy older people and caused more bleeding [1][2]. It enrolled 19,114 healthy participants, mostly over 70, who took either 100 mg of aspirin daily or a placebo for about five years [1]. Rates of coronary heart disease, nonfatal heart attack and ischemic stroke were similar in the two groups, and the combined cardiovascular outcome was not significantly lower with aspirin [1][3]. Major hemorrhage was more common with aspirin (8.6 vs 6.2 events per 1,000 person-years; HR 1.38) [1]. Aspirin also did not extend disability-free survival. The aspirin group had a higher death rate, which the researchers linked to more cancer in that group [1]. The findings apply to healthy people with no existing indication. They do not apply to people already taking aspirin after a heart attack or stroke, and they did not address people under 65 [1].

Other large primary-prevention trials point the same way. ARRIVE, in average-risk adults, showed no difference in cardiovascular events between aspirin users and nonusers. ASCEND, in adults with diabetes, found fewer serious vascular events with aspirin but also more major bleeding [4]. Based on this evidence, the US Preventive Services Task Force proposed recommending against starting aspirin for primary prevention in adults 60 and older (Grade D), a change from its 2016 position [4][5]. Note that the search results confirmed the 2021 draft wording. I did not retrieve the final 2022 statement itself, though an ACC summary of the 2022 USPSTF report shows the change went forward [6].

question: How common is long COVID, and what are its most frequently reported symptoms?
answer:
Estimates of how common long COVID is vary widely because studies use different definitions, populations and time periods. One pooled analysis of 35 studies from 19 countries (about 159,000 participants) put prevalence at roughly 29%, higher before the Omicron wave (about 35.5%) than during it (about 22.8%) [1]. Population surveys give lower numbers. In 2022 CDC data, 6.9% of US adults (about 18 million) said they had ever had long COVID and 3.4% (about 8.8 million) said they currently had it [2]. Women and adults aged 35 to 49 reported it more often [2]. Later CDC-linked figures put current prevalence near 6% to 7% in 2023 to 2024 surveys [3]. A 2026 analysis of 2022 to 2024 data found that among previously infected adults, ever-long-COVID fell from 17.7% to 13.7% and current long COVID fell from 8.6% to 5.5% [4]. These figures use different denominators, so they are not directly comparable.

Fatigue is the symptom most consistently reported. A 2025 meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies found fatigue (41.0%) and dyspnoea (22.5%) were the most common [5]. A review across variant periods found fatigue first, followed by brain fog, shortness of breath and sleep problems [1]. UK Office for National Statistics data ranked fatigue first (547,000 people), then shortness of breath (405,000), muscle ache (313,000) and difficulty concentrating (285,000) [6]. Other commonly listed symptoms include joint pain, headache, cough, chest pain and changes in smell or taste [2].

question: What is lecanemab, and how much did it slow cognitive decline in its phase 3 trial?
answer:
Lecanemab (brand name Leqembi, from Eisai and Biogen) is an antibody given by intravenous infusion that targets beta-amyloid and removes it from the brain [1]. It is meant for people in the early stages of Alzheimer's disease, meaning mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia with confirmed elevated amyloid. It does not cure the disease [1]. The FDA first approved it in January 2023 under the accelerated pathway, based on a phase 2b study and interim phase 3 data, and it has since received traditional approval [1][2].

In the phase 3 Clarity AD trial, 1,795 people with early Alzheimer's received lecanemab (10 mg/kg every two weeks) or placebo for 18 months [3][4]. On the primary outcome, the CDR-SB scale, patients on lecanemab worsened by 1.21 points on average versus 1.66 on placebo [3]. That gap is the 27% relative slowing of decline, which is an absolute difference of about 0.45 points on the 18-point scale [3][4]. The separation appeared as early as six months and widened at each 3-month assessment [3]. Experts disagree about whether a difference this size is clinically meaningful [3], and one independent evidence review rated the treatment 'Promising but Inconclusive' [5].

The main safety issue was brain swelling (ARIA-E), seen in 12.5% of the lecanemab group versus 1.7% on placebo. Infusion reactions occurred in 26.4% versus 7.4% [3]. The full results were presented at CTAD 2022 and published in the New England Journal of Medicine [3][6].

question: How much has global average temperature risen since pre-industrial times, and what was the warmest year on record?
answer:
Global average temperature is now roughly 1.5 degrees C above pre-industrial levels. The exact figure depends on the dataset and baseline. The warmest year on record is 2024, according to the search results, which cover through 2025. 2026 is still in progress, so I did not find a final ranking for it.

Copernicus reported 2024 as 1.60 C above the pre-industrial level, the first calendar year to exceed 1.5 C [1]. The WMO's consolidated analysis of six datasets gave 1.55 C (plus or minus 0.13 C) above the 1850 to 1900 baseline [2]. NOAA's figure was lower, at 1.46 C above its 1850 to 1900 average [3]. The Met Office noted that 2024 beat the previous record year, 2023 (1.46 C), by 0.12 C. It also cautioned that one year above 1.5 C is not a breach of the Paris Agreement 1.5 C guard rail, which refers to a longer-term average [4]. The 10 warmest years since 1850 have all occurred in the last decade [4].

2025 then ranked third-warmest in Copernicus's final assessment, at 1.47 C above pre-industrial, just 0.01 C cooler than 2023 [5][6]. The WMO said two of the eight datasets it analysed put 2025 second and the other six put it third [5]. The 2023 to 2025 three-year average exceeded 1.5 C for the first time [5][6].

question: What did the James Webb Space Telescope find about the atmosphere of exoplanet K2-18 b?
answer:
JWST's 2023 observations of K2-18 b, a sub-Neptune in its star's habitable zone, detected methane and carbon dioxide in its atmosphere. The team found no ammonia, which they read as consistent with a hydrogen-rich atmosphere over a possible water ocean [1][2]. The spectra came from two instruments, NIRISS and NIRSpec, and only two observations. The team also reported a weak, tentative hint of dimethyl sulfide (DMS), a molecule that on Earth is produced mainly by life [2][3]. The lead researchers said the data were not enough to say whether the planet is habitable [2].

The DMS claim has been disputed since. In April 2025 Madhusudhan's team reported tentative DMS/DMDS signatures at about 3 sigma in new mid-infrared MIRI data, well below the 5-sigma standard for a confirmed discovery [4]. Independent reanalyses did not support it. A joint analysis of NIRISS, NIRSpec and MIRI data concluded there is insufficient evidence for DMS or DMDS in the atmosphere [5]. A separate reanalysis of the 2023 near-infrared data confirmed methane at about 4 sigma but found no statistically significant evidence for CO2 or DMS [6]. Other critics found no clear molecular signatures beyond insignificant hints [4][7]. Most of these reanalyses are preprints, and I did not find a published rebuttal from the original team, so the DMS question remains unresolved [4][7].

question: How much of the Great Barrier Reef was affected by the most recent mass bleaching event?
answer: The most recent mass bleaching event I could confirm is the 2025 event, which AIMS counts as the sixth mass coral bleaching on the Great Barrier Reef since 2016 [1]. It was patchy rather than reef-wide. Aerial surveys in March 2025 concentrated on the Northern GBR and parts of the Central GBR north of Townsville, and none were flown south of Townsville because heat stress there was lower [1]. In the 2024-25 Reef Snapshot, 41% of the 162 inshore and mid-shelf reefs surveyed had medium to high bleaching prevalence. Across all 258 reefs surveyed, only 9% had very high prevalence and none had extremely high prevalence [2]. AIMS says bleaching prevalence in 2025 was more moderate than in the 2024, 2016 and 2017 events [1]. For comparison, an AIMS news item attributes a figure of 73% of surveyed reefs with prevalent bleaching to the 2024 aerial surveys [5]. The 2025 event still caused sharp coral loss in the north. Hard coral cover on the Northern GBR fell 24.8%, from 39.8% in 2024 to 30.0%, the largest annual decline ever recorded for that region [1]. More recently, GBRMPA described a regional bleaching event in the Northern region that became apparent in March 2026, with only localised low-level bleaching elsewhere [3]. AIMS's 2025-26 survey of 121 reefs found limited impacts from the 2025 event and the early-2026 regional event, and northern coral cover rose to 35.1% [4]. I did not rely on an unverified website claiming 91% of reefs were bleached in 2026, because it conflicts with the official GBRMPA and AIMS material.

question: What is the current concentration of CO2 in the atmosphere and how fast is it rising?
answer: The most recent NOAA Mauna Loa monthly figure I found is June 2026 at 431.44 ppm, compared with 429.61 ppm in June 2025. That is a year-over-year rise of about 1.8 ppm [1]. Monthly values swing with the seasons, so comparing the same month across years is the fairest measure. I could not find readings later than June 2026, so this is not an October 2026 value. For the annual picture, the UK Met Office forecasts that the 2026 Mauna Loa annual average will be 2.37 ± 0.55 ppm higher than 2025, at about 429.4 ± 0.6 ppm [2]. The Met Office says the average annual rise observed at Mauna Loa was 2.61 ppm in the first half of the 2020s [2]. It also says the yearly rise has grown over the six decades of the record, mainly because of fossil fuel burning [2]. The Met Office concludes that the rise will remain too fast to track global climate targets in 2026 [3]. The year-to-year rise varies with natural factors, which is why single-year readings (about 1.8 ppm observed versus about 2.4 ppm forecast) differ [1][2].

question: What happened during the first crewed flight test of Boeing's Starliner?
answer: Starliner's Crew Flight Test lifted off on June 5, 2024 carrying NASA astronauts Butch Wilmore and Suni Williams, and was meant to be a short trip to the International Space Station [1][2]. Problems began on the way. Five of the capsule's 28 reaction control thrusters shut down before docking. The astronauts flew the vehicle manually and engineers recovered four of the five, with the fifth deactivated for the rest of the mission [1]. Helium leaks in the propulsion system were also found: one small leak before launch and several more after liftoff [1][3]. NASA and Boeing said there was enough helium to get home, but the cause was unclear and a faulty seal was suspected [1]. The crew's stay stretched from days to months while engineers tested the thrusters. After more than two months of investigation, NASA judged that returning the astronauts on Starliner was too risky and sent the capsule home empty [3][4]. It undocked on September 6, 2024 and landed uncrewed at White Sands, New Mexico, at 10:01 p.m. MDT [3][4]. Wilmore and Williams came back in March 2025 aboard a SpaceX Crew Dragon, after about nine months in space. They rode in two seats left empty on the Crew-9 mission [5]. NASA said at the time it did not consider the test flight a failure [6]. In February 2026, though, a NASA investigation classified the flight as a Type A mishap, the agency's most serious category, and cited management failures as well as technical ones [7]. The technical root-cause work is reportedly still open, and NASA has said it will not fly another crew on Starliner until the causes are understood and fixed. The next Starliner flight is planned as an uncrewed cargo mission [7][8].

question: How much electricity does training and running large AI models use compared with other data center workloads?
answer: AI is a large and fast-growing slice of data center power, but still a minority. Our World in Data, drawing on IEA figures, estimates that non-AI data centers used about two-thirds of the total and AI-focused ones the remaining third [1]. One industry summary puts global data center use at about 415 TWh in 2024, roughly 1.5% of world electricity, and estimates that US AI-specific servers used 53-76 TWh that year [2]. Berkeley Lab estimates US data centers used about 4.4% of US electricity in 2023 (around 176 TWh). It says their demand more than doubled between 2017 and 2023, largely from AI servers, and could reach 6.7% to 12% of US electricity by 2028 [3]. The IEA projects global data center demand of about 945 TWh by 2030, nearly 3% of global electricity, and says demand from AI-optimised data centers will more than quadruple [4]. On training versus running models, Our World in Data notes that tech companies rarely publish this data. Based on the estimates available, it says demand is likely dominated by inference, meaning serving user queries, rather than training [1]. Some secondary sources put inference at 80-90% of AI energy use, but I could not verify the data behind those claims. The split also depends on how often a model is retrained and how heavily it is used [1]. These numbers are estimates, and scope (global versus US, with or without cooling and other overhead) differs between sources.

question: What is the status of the ITER fusion project and when is first plasma now expected?
answer: ITER no longer plans a stand-alone first plasma milestone. Under the 2016 baseline, first plasma was due in December 2025 [1]. The 2024 re-baseline dropped that target and replaced it with a Start of Research Operation in 2034. That phase uses hydrogen and deuterium-deuterium plasmas, to be followed by full magnetic energy in 2036 and deuterium-tritium operation in 2039 [2][3]. The delay was reported with about 5 billion euros in extra cost [3][4]. In practice, 2034 is the date that now stands in for first plasma. Construction is progressing against the new baseline. At the 38th ITER Council on 25-26 June 2026, members praised project execution under Baseline 2024. ITER reported 192 Level 1 milestones achieved against 188 planned by the end of June 2026 [5]. ITER said two-thirds of the tokamak core was in place by June 2026 [6]. The ninth and final vacuum vessel sector reached the Cadarache site on 2 October 2026, so all the major core tokamak components are on site. Six of the nine sector modules are in the tokamak pit, and the final module is expected to be installed around mid-2027 [7][8]. Reports after the final sector's arrival say the 2034, 2036 and 2039 targets are unchanged [7]. Early coverage of the baseline differed on whether research operations would begin in 2033 or 2034, so the exact year depends on the source and definition. ITER's own materials say 2034.

question: What are the main differences between the EU AI Act's risk categories?
answer:
The EU AI Act sorts AI systems into four tiers, and the obligations get lighter as the risk level falls [1][2].

- Unacceptable risk: these systems are banned outright. They threaten safety, fundamental rights or democratic values, and Article 5 lists the prohibited practices, with limited law-enforcement exceptions. Social scoring is the standard example. The bans have applied since February 2025 [1]. Breaches carry the top penalty tier, up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover [3].
- High risk: these systems are allowed but face the heaviest obligations. Annex III covers uses such as employment, credit, education and biometrics, and medical-device safety components also fall here. Obligations include risk management, documentation, logging, human oversight, conformity assessment and EU database registration [1][3][4]. The EU has approved a delay. Annex III duties now apply from 2 December 2027 and Annex I duties from 2 August 2028 [3][4].
- Limited risk: the main duty is transparency under Article 50. Users must be told they are dealing with an AI, such as a chatbot, AI-generated content must be machine-readable marked, and deepfakes must be labelled. No conformity assessment or database registration is needed [1][3][5]. One source says Article 50 has applied since 2 August 2026, though sources differ on some details [3][5].
- Minimal risk: this covers most systems, such as spam filters and AI-enabled video games. The Act sets no specific mandatory obligations for them, though existing consumer-protection and liability rules still apply [1].

Other breaches, including Article 50, carry fines of up to EUR 15 million or 3% of turnover [3]. A system that serves both high-risk and minimal-risk functions is classified at the highest applicable tier [1]. These are secondary summaries, so check exact dates and wording against the Official Journal text [3].

question: What did the US Department of Justice argue in its antitrust case against Google search, and what did the court decide?
answer:
The DOJ argued that Google illegally maintained a monopoly in general search by paying for default placement. At the May 2024 closing arguments, prosecutors pointed to multibillion-dollar payments to wireless carriers and device makers. Witnesses testified that Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 and paid Apple alone about $20 billion in 2022 to be the default search engine. The DOJ said these payments helped Google keep rivals out and protect its position [1][2]. DOJ lawyers cited a share of about 89.2% of general search, above 70% since 2009. They said default status gives Google more queries than rivals, which improves its algorithms and makes it harder for competitors to attract users [1]. Google replied that the payments help support the Android ecosystem, which competes with Apple's iPhone [1].

In August 2024, Judge Amit Mehta found Google liable under Section 2 of the Sherman Act. He held that Google has monopoly power in the markets for general search and general search text advertising. He also held that its exclusive agreements with Apple, Samsung, Verizon and others, for which it paid tens of billions of dollars, helped it maintain that dominance for more than a decade [3].

The remedies decision came on 2 September 2025 and was mostly behavioral. The court declined to order divestiture of Chrome or Android. It barred exclusive distribution contracts, though Google may still pay distributors such as Apple or Samsung for default placement, and it limited default deals to one year [4][5]. It also required Google to share certain data, including parts of its search index and user-interaction data, with competitors [5][6]. Mehta said the remedies he chose were influenced by competition from AI search startups [5].

The case is still being litigated. Google appealed in January 2026 to the D.C. Circuit, seeking to overturn both the liability ruling and the remedies. The DOJ and states cross-appealed, arguing Mehta erred in rejecting a ban on Google's search-related payments to distributors [7][8]. I found no reporting of an appeals decision.

question: How many people use ChatGPT weekly according to OpenAI's most recent figures?
answer:
The most recent figure I found is about 1.2 billion weekly users. Secondary coverage says OpenAI cited it at DevDay on 29 September 2026. I could not reach OpenAI's own recap, so treat that number as likely but unverified [1]. Some of the pages reporting 1.2 billion are low-quality aggregators, and some describe it as covering OpenAI's products collectively rather than ChatGPT alone [1][2].

Earlier milestones show the growth. OpenAI reported 900 million weekly users in late February 2026, together with more than 50 million paying subscribers [5]. question: What is the market share of Android versus iOS worldwide and in the United States?
answer:
Android leads worldwide and iOS leads in the United States. These figures are usage shares from StatCounter, which measures mobile web traffic rather than devices owned or sold.

Worldwide, StatCounter's September 2026 mobile OS page shows Android at about 69.3% and iOS at about 30.7% [1]. A secondary report puts the January-to-September 2026 average at about 68.5% Android and 31.3% iOS [2]. iOS has gained share since 2025. A 2025 roundup cited roughly 72.7% Android and 26.9% iOS [2].

In the United States, StatCounter's September 2026 page shows iOS at about 53.6% and Android at about 46.4% [3]. The US figure moves a lot from month to month. Reports for earlier months of 2026 put iOS between roughly 58% and 61% [3][4]. Those earlier-month numbers are secondhand, so check StatCounter's pages for the exact current values [3][4].

Share of sales or shipments differs from share of usage. One report cites Counterpoint data putting Q2 2026 US smartphone sales at roughly 51% iOS and 49% Android [4].

question: What happened in the CrowdStrike outage of July 2024 and how many devices were affected?
answer:
On 19 July 2024, a faulty content update to CrowdStrike's Falcon sensor crashed Windows machines around the world. CrowdStrike pushed the update at 04:09 UTC and fixed the problem by 05:27 UTC. Windows hosts running Falcon sensor version 7.11 or above that were online in that window were affected, and Mac and Linux systems were not [1][2]. Affected PCs showed the Blue Screen of Death, and airlines, banks and other businesses were disrupted [1][3].

Microsoft estimated that about 8.5 million Windows devices were affected, which it said was less than 1% of all Windows machines [3][4].

The trigger was a faulty update to Channel File 291. CrowdStrike's analysis blamed a validation gap. One engineering analysis describes a detection template that declared 21 inputs while the sensor code supplied 20, and a new matching criterion then exposed an unchecked array access in the kernel-mode content interpreter. The early "file full of zeros" explanation reportedly did not hold up [5][6]. Recovery was slow because IT teams often had to fix each machine individually. By 26 July, CEO George Kurtz said 97% of Windows sensors were back online [2][7].

Cost estimates vary by source. Delta alone reported about $500-550 million in costs, and Parametrix put losses for six Fortune 500 airlines at about $860 million. No authoritative global figure exists [6].

question: What are the key specifications of Apple's M5 chip?
answer: The M5 is Apple's base-tier chip, announced in October 2025 [1][2]. Its CPU has up to 10 cores (reported as up to four performance cores plus six efficiency cores), and Apple claims about 15% faster multithreaded performance than the M4 [2]. The GPU has 10 cores, each with its own neural accelerator, so AI work can run on the GPU as well as on the 16-core Neural Engine [3][2]. Apple claims more than 4x the peak GPU compute for AI compared with the M4, and roughly 30% more graphics performance [3][2]. Ray-tracing performance is claimed to be up to 45% better [4]. Unified memory bandwidth rises by nearly 30%, to 153GB/s from the M4's 120GB/s, and configurations go up to 32GB of unified memory [2][4]. Nearly all of these figures are Apple's own claims relative to the M4, and I did not check independent benchmarks.

question: How does Perplexity cite sources in its answers, and has it faced lawsuits from publishers?
answer:
Perplexity works as a retrieval-first answer engine. It runs a live web search for each query and then has a language model write an answer from the pages it retrieved [1]. One third-party guide says it retrieves roughly 5-15 sources and shows about 3-8 of them as numbered citations. The model is constrained to cite from that filtered pool, and each claim is linked to one or more numbered sources [1][2]. The citations appear inline as numbered footnotes that link to source cards [2]. Most of this description comes from SEO and marketing blogs, not Perplexity's own documentation, so the specific numbers are rough.

Yes, Perplexity has been sued by several publishers. Dow Jones and the New York Post sued in October 2024 over alleged copying of their content, after earlier raising the issue with Perplexity and offering to discuss a license [3][8]. Encyclopedia Britannica and Merriam-Webster sued in September 2025, and one report says their complaint also objects to Perplexity attributing AI hallucinations to Britannica [4]. The New York Times and the Chicago Tribune sued in December 2025, alleging verbatim reuse of their material [5][6]. Perplexity's position is that it does not scrape data to build foundation models. It says it indexes web pages and provides factual citations [8]. Critics note that its marketing promotes letting users 'skip the links' [6].

In the Dow Jones case, a New York federal court in August 2025 denied Perplexity's bid to dismiss or transfer the case, so it continues [7]. I found no 2026 rulings or settlements in these results, so check the court dockets for current status.

question: What is retrieval-augmented generation and what are its main failure modes?
answer:
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pairs a retrieval step with a generative model. The system first fetches documents relevant to the user's query from a data store, and the language model then writes its answer using them. The aim is to reduce hallucinated responses [1][2].

Retrieval is usually the most common point of failure. Practitioners report that most problems start in retrieval rather than in the model. Typical causes are the retriever returning the wrong passages, chunking that loses context, a stale or incomplete knowledge base, and no evaluation in place [3]. The best-known taxonomy is Barnett et al.'s 'seven failure points', drawn from case studies in research, education and biomedical settings [1][4]. A third-party summary of it lists these:
1. Missing content: the answer is not in the document store.
2. Missed top-ranked documents: relevant documents are not ranked high enough to be retrieved.
3. Not in context: key information does not fit in the context window after consolidation.
4. Not extracted: the model fails to pull the answer out of the context, often because of noise or contradictory information.
5. Wrong format: the model ignores a requested structure such as a table or list.
6. Incorrect specificity: the answer is too general or too specific.
7. Incomplete: the answer omits information that was in the context [4].
I could not confirm the exact wording of items 6 and 7 against the paper itself.

A 2026 TrustNLP paper extends this to 33 failure modes across seven pipeline stages: ingestion, retrieval, generation, evaluation, deployment and agentic orchestration. The same source set reports that 12 of the 33 have no dedicated peer-reviewed empirical evidence [5]. Vendor guides, such as Splunk's, add production concerns like hallucination and security to the testing checklist [6]. RAG reduces hallucination but does not eliminate it, because the model can still answer wrongly even when retrieval works [7]. The paper's own takeaway is that validating a RAG system is only really feasible during operation [1]. Teams should also keep retrieval errors separable from generation errors. Without chunk attribution, an audit cannot tell which one caused a wrong answer [7].

question: What was the US inflation rate for the most recent month reported, and how does it compare with a year earlier?
answer:
The most recent report I found is for September 2026, released October 14, 2026. Headline CPI-U rose 3.7% over the 12 months ending in September, up from 3.4% in August [1][2]. Core inflation (all items less food and energy) was 2.6% over the year. Energy was up 20.4%, driven mainly by gasoline, and food was up 2.5% [1][2]. On a seasonally adjusted basis, prices rose 0.6% in the month [1].

A year earlier, CPI-U was up 3.0% over the 12 months ending September 2025, after 2.9% in August 2025 [3]. So the headline annual rate is about 0.7 percentage points higher than a year ago, and it has accelerated for two straight months. As far as my searches show, the October 2026 figure had not yet been published. I did not open the BLS release page directly, so check bls.gov to confirm the figures.

question: How did the Federal Reserve change interest rates over the past year?
answer:
Over the roughly 12 months to early November 2026, the Fed made one cut, then one hike. Otherwise it held rates steady.

The last of three cuts in 2025 came on December 10, 2025, when the Fed lowered the federal funds target range by 25 basis points to 3.50%-3.75%. The vote was 9-3 [1][2]. The first two of those 2025 cuts came earlier, in September and October, and the October cut falls just outside a strict 12-month window. They took the range down from 4.25%-4.50% [2].

The Fed then held rates through the first half of 2026. It held in January [3] and in March, when Governor Stephen Miran dissented in favor of a cut [4]. It also held in June and July [5][6]. I could not confirm the outcome of the April meeting from my results. In July the vote was 9-3, with three regional presidents preferring a hike [5].

On September 16, 2026, the Fed raised the range by 25 basis points to 3.75%-4.00%. This was its first hike since 2023, and the vote was unanimous [7][8]. On October 28, 2026, it held at 3.75%-4.00%. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented in favor of another quarter-point hike, and futures markets were pricing about an 85% chance of a hike in December [9].

Some reference pages still show the older 3.50%-3.75% range, so they appear out of date.
